source: 「若正說佛子從佛口生，從法化生，得佛法分者，則我身是也。所以者何？我是佛子，從佛口生，從法化生，得佛法分，以少方便，得禪、解脫、三昧、正受。譬如轉輪聖王長太子，雖未灌頂，已得王法，不勤方便，能得五欲功德。我亦如是，為佛之子，不勤方便，得禪、解脫、三昧、正受，於一日中，世尊以神通力三至我所，三教授我，以大人處所建立於我。」
A: "If one were to speak correctly of a son of the Buddha (buddhaputra) as born from the Buddha’s mouth, born through transformation by the Dharma (dharma), and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma, then that person is myself. Why is this? I am a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, born through transformation by the Dharma, and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma; with little effort, I have attained meditative absorption (dhyāna), liberation (vimokṣa), concentration (samādhi), and correct reception (samāpatti). It is like the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin): although he has not yet been anointed, he already possesses the royal law and, without strenuous effort, is able to obtain the merits of the five desires. I am also like this; as a son of the Buddha, without strenuous effort, I have attained meditative absorption, liberation, concentration, and correct reception. Within a single day, the World-Honored One (bhagavat) came to me three times through his supernatural power (ṛddhi), instructed me three times, and established me in the station of a great man."
B: "If one were to speak correctly, saying that a son of the Buddha (buddha-putra) is born from the mouth of the Buddha, born through transformation by the Dharma (dharma), and obtains a portion of the Buddha-Dharma, then I am that person. Why is this? I am a son of the Buddha, born from the mouth of the Buddha, born through transformation by the Dharma, and have obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma, having attained through little effort the meditative absorption (dhyāna), liberation (vimokṣa), concentration (samādhi), and correct reception (samāpatti). It is like the eldest prince (kumāra) of a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), who, although not yet anointed, already possesses the royal law and, without strenuous effort, is able to obtain the merits (guṇa) of the five desires. I am also like this; being a son of the Buddha, without strenuous effort, I have attained meditative absorption, liberation, concentration, and correct reception. In a single day, the Blessed One (bhagavant) came to me three times through his power of supernormal knowledge (abhijñā), instructed me three times, and established me in the place of a great man."

source: 是出世間無分別智，斷世間故，名「出世間」。二取隨眠是世間本，唯此能斷獨得「出」名。或「出世」名依二義立，謂體無漏及證真如，此智具斯二種義故，獨名「出世」，餘智不然，即十地中無分別智。
A: This is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna); it is called "supramundane" (lokottara) because it severs the mundane. The latencies (anuśaya) of the twofold grasping are the root of the mundane, and because only this wisdom can sever them, it alone receives the name "supramundane." Alternatively, the name "supramundane" is established based on two meanings: its essence is untainted (anāsrava), and it realizes True Suchness (tathatā). Because this wisdom possesses these two meanings, it alone is called "supramundane," whereas other forms of wisdom are not; this refers to the non-conceptual wisdom within the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
B: This is supramundane (lokottara) non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna); it is called "supramundane" because it severs the mundane (loka). The latencies (anuśaya) of the twofold grasping are the root of the mundane, and because only this wisdom can sever them, it alone receives the name "supramundane." Alternatively, the name "supramundane" is established based on two meanings (artha): its essence is untainted (anāsrava), and it realizes True Suchness (tathatā). Because this wisdom possesses these two kinds (dvividha) of meanings, it alone is called "supramundane," whereas other forms of wisdom are not; this refers to the non-conceptual wisdom within the ten stages (daśan-bhūmi).

source: 《瑜伽論》說：若任運生一切煩惱，皆於三受現行可得。若通一切識身者，遍與一切根相應；不通一切識身者，意地一切根相應。《雜集論》說：若欲界繫任運煩惱，發惡行者，亦是不善。所餘皆是有覆無記。
A: The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra states: if all afflictions (kleśa) arise spontaneously, they can all be found manifesting in connection with the three feelings (vedanā). If they are common to all groups of consciousness (vijñāna-kāya), they are universally associated with all faculties (indriya); if they are not common to all groups of consciousness, they are associated with all faculties in the mental ground (manobhūmi). The Abhidharmasamuccaya states: if spontaneous afflictions bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyuj) produce evil conduct, they are also unwholesome (akuśala); all others are obscured and indeterminate (nivṛta-avyākṛta).
B: The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra states: If all afflictions (kleśa) arise spontaneously (sahaja), they can all be found manifesting in connection with the three feelings (vedanā). If they are common to all groups of consciousness (vijñāna-kāya), they are universally associated with all faculties (indriya); if they are not common to all groups of consciousness, they are associated with all faculties in the mental ground (manobhūmi). The Abhidharmasamuccaya states: If spontaneous afflictions bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) produce evil conduct (akuśala-karman), they are also unwholesome (akuśala); all others are obscured and indeterminate (nivṛtāvyākṛta).

source: 前、中、後際，生死輪迴，不待外緣，既由內識，淨法相續，應知亦然。謂無始來，依附本識，有、無漏種，由轉識等，數數熏發，漸漸增勝，乃至究竟，得成佛時，轉捨本來雜染識種，轉得始起清淨種識，任持一切功德種子。由本願力，盡未來際，起諸妙用，相續無窮。
A: Regarding the past, present, and future, the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) does not depend on external conditions; since it arises from internal consciousness (vijñāna), the continuity of pure phenomena (dharma) should be understood in the same way. From beginningless time, there have adhered to the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) both tainted and untainted seeds (bīja). Through the transforming consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) and others, these are repeatedly perfumed and activated, gradually increasing in strength until, at the point of ultimate attainment—when one becomes a Buddha—one abandons the originally defiled seeds of consciousness and transforms them to obtain the newly arisen pure seeds of consciousness, which sustain all seeds of merit (guṇa). By the power of original vows (pūrva-praṇidhāna), various marvelous functions arise until the end of future time in an endless succession.
B: Regarding the past, present, and future (apara-anta), the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) does not depend on external conditions; since it arises from internal consciousness, the continuity (saṃtāna) of pure phenomena should be understood in the same way. It is said that from beginningless time, there have adhered to the fundamental consciousness both tainted and untainted seeds (bīja), which, through the transforming consciousness and so forth, are repeatedly perfumed and stimulated, gradually increasing in strength until the ultimate (niṣṭhā) attainment of Buddhahood. At that time, one transforms and abandons the originally defiled consciousness-seeds and transforms and attains the newly arisen pure consciousness-seeds, which sustain the seeds of all virtues (sarva-guṇa). By the power of the original vows (praṇidhāna-bala), until the end of future time (aparānta-koṭi), various marvelous functions arise in an endless succession.

source: 論曰：若住律儀，由勝煩惱作殺縛等諸不善業，由此便發不善無表；住不律儀，由淳淨信作禮佛等諸勝善業，由此亦發諸善無表。乃至此二心未斷來，所發無表恒時相續，然其初念唯成現在，自茲以後通成過現。已辯無表，成表云何？頌曰：
A: The treatise says: If one who dwells in discipline (saṃvara) performs unwholesome actions (akuśala-karman) such as killing or binding due to powerful defilements (kleśa), they consequently produce unwholesome non-informative matter (avijñapti); if one who dwells in indiscipline (asaṃvara) performs superior wholesome actions such as bowing to the Buddha due to pure faith (śraddhā), they consequently produce wholesome non-informative matter. As long as these two types of mind are not severed, the non-informative matter produced continues uninterruptedly; however, its first moment exists only in the present, while from that point onward it exists in both the past and the present. Having explained non-informative matter, how is informative matter (vijñapti) accomplished? The verse says:
B: The treatise says: If one who dwells in discipline (saṃvara) performs unwholesome actions (akuśala-karman) such as killing or binding due to powerful defilements (kleśa), they consequently produce unwholesome non-informative matter (avijñapti). If one who dwells in indiscipline (asaṃvara) performs superior wholesome actions (kuśala-karman) such as bowing to the Buddha due to pure faith (prasāda), they consequently also produce wholesome non-informative matter. Until these two types of mind are severed, the non-informative matter that is produced continues constantly (saṃtāna); however, its first moment exists only in the present (vartamāna), while from that point onward it exists in both the past and the present. Having already explained non-informative matter, how is informative matter accomplished? The verse says:

source: 論曰：如是五種設是異生，但施亦能招無量果。住最後有，名最後生。法師四田中，是何田所攝？是恩田攝。所以者何？為諸世間大善友故、無明所盲者能施慧眼故、開示世間安危事故、令有情生起無漏法身故。以要說者，善說法師乃至能為佛所作事故，於彼行施便招無量果。欲知諸業輕重相者，應知輕重略由六因。其六者何？頌曰：
A: The treatise says: Even if these five kinds of beings are ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), giving to them can still bring about immeasurable fruit. One who dwells in their final existence (caramabhavika) is called one who has reached their final birth (caramabhavika). Among the four fields of merit, in which field is the Dharma-preacher (dharmabhāṇaka) included? He is included in the field of gratitude. Why is this? Because he is a great virtuous friend to all the world, because he can bestow the eye of wisdom upon those blinded by ignorance (avidyā), because he reveals the matters of safety and peril in the world (loka), and because he enables sentient beings (sattva) to give rise to the untainted (anāsrava) Dharma-body (dharmakāya). In short, because a skilled Dharma-preacher can even perform the work (kṛtya) of a Buddha, giving to him brings about immeasurable fruit. If one wishes to know the characteristics of the lightness or heaviness of various actions (karman), one should know that lightness and heaviness are briefly due to six causes. What are those six? The verse says:
B: The treatise says: Even if these five types are ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), giving to them can still bring about immeasurable fruit. Those who dwell in their final existence (caramabhava) are called those in their final birth. Among the four fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra), which field does the teacher of the Dharma (dharmabhāṇaka) belong to? He is included in the field of gratitude (kṛtajñakṣetra). Why is this? Because he is a great virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) to all the world, because he bestows the eye of wisdom (prajñācakṣus) upon those blinded by ignorance (avidyā), because he reveals the matters of safety and peril in the world, and because he enables sentient beings to give rise to the untainted Dharma-body (anāsravadharmakāya). In short, because a teacher who speaks well is even able to perform the work of a Buddha, giving to him brings about immeasurable fruit. If one wishes to know the characteristics of the lightness and heaviness of all actions (karman), one should know that lightness and heaviness are determined by six causes. What are the six? The verse says:

source: 復有二種：謂利自、他所修勝行，隨意樂力一切皆通自他利行，依別相說，六到彼岸、菩提分等，自利行攝；四種攝事、四無量等，一切皆是利他行攝。如是等行差別無邊，皆是此中所修勝行。
A: Furthermore, there are two kinds: namely, the superior practices (viśeṣa-caryā) cultivated for the benefit of oneself and others. Through the power of intention (āśaya), all practices are generally capable of benefiting both oneself and others; however, speaking in terms of their distinct characteristics, the six perfections (pāramitā), the aids to enlightenment (bodhi-pakṣya), and so forth are categorized as practices for self-benefit (sva-artha), while the four means of attraction (saṃgraha-vastu), the four immeasurables (catur-apramāṇa), and so forth are all categorized as practices for the benefit of others (para-artha). Such diverse practices are boundless (ananta), and all are the superior practices cultivated herein.
B: Furthermore, there are two kinds: namely, the superior practices (viśeṣacaryā) cultivated for the benefit of self and others. Through the power of one’s intention (āśaya), all practices are generally understood as benefiting both self and others. Speaking in terms of their distinct characteristics, the six perfections (pāramitā), the aids to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), and so forth are categorized as practices for self-benefit (svārthacaryā); the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), the four immeasurables (apramāṇa), and so forth are all categorized as practices for the benefit of others (parārthacaryā). Such diverse practices are boundless, and all are the superior practices cultivated in this context.

source: 論曰：由田勝者，聞有苾芻於僧眾中作女人語，彼於現世轉作女人。此等傳聞其類非一。由意勝者，聞有黃門救脫諸牛黃門事故，彼於現世轉作丈夫。此等傳聞事亦非一。或生此地永離此地染，於此地中諸善不善業。於異熟定位不定者，此業必能招現法果。若有餘位順定受業，彼必定無永離染義，必於餘位受異熟果。若於異熟亦不定者，永離染故不受異熟。何田起業定即受耶？頌曰：
A:
The treatise says: Regarding the excellence of the field, it is heard that there was a monk (bhikṣu) who spoke like a woman in the midst of the monastic community, and because of that, he was transformed into a woman in his present lifetime. Such reports are not singular. Regarding the excellence of intention, it is heard that there was a eunuch (paṇḍaka) who saved cows from the affairs of eunuchs, and because of that, he was transformed into a man in his present lifetime. Such reports are also not singular.

Or, one may be born in this realm and permanently abandon the defilements (kleśa) of this realm, regarding the wholesome and unwholesome actions (karman) within this realm. For an action that is certain in its ripening (vipāka) but uncertain in its timing, this action will inevitably bring about a result in the present lifetime. If there is an action that is certain to be experienced in another lifetime, it certainly lacks the meaning of having permanently abandoned defilements, and it will necessarily experience its ripening in another lifetime. If the ripening itself is also uncertain, then because one has permanently abandoned defilements, one will not experience the ripening. From what field does an action arise such that it is certain to be experienced? The verse says:
B:
The treatise says: Regarding those superior in terms of the field, it is heard that a bhikṣu (monk) spoke to the community of monks using the speech of a woman, and in this very lifetime he was transformed into a woman. Such reports are not singular. Regarding those superior in terms of intention, it is heard that a eunuch (paṇḍaka) saved some cattle from a eunuch-related incident, and in this very lifetime he was transformed into a man (puruṣa). Such reports are also not singular.

As for wholesome and unwholesome karman (action) performed in this state, if one is born into this state and permanently detaches from the defilements (vairāgya) of this state, then for that karman which is uncertain regarding the timing of its ripening (vipāka), that karman will inevitably bring about a result in the present lifetime (dṛṣṭadharma). If there is other karman that is certain to be experienced in a subsequent state, then for that person there is no meaning in having permanently detached from defilements, for they will certainly experience the ripening in a subsequent state. If the ripening itself is also uncertain, then because one has permanently detached from defilements, one will not experience the ripening.

What is the field from which karman arises such that it is certain to be experienced? The gāthā (verse) says:

source: 論曰：無從果退中間命終，退已須臾必還得故。如契經說：苾芻當知，如是多聞諸聖弟子退失正念，速復還能令所退起盡沒滅離。若謂不然，修梵行果應非安隱可委信處。又住果位所不應為違果事業，由慚增故於暫退時亦必不造，譬如壯士雖蹶不仆。如上所言，有練根得無學有學，正練根時各幾無間、幾解脫道？何性攝？何所依？頌曰：
A:
The Commentary says: There is no death in the interval for one who has fallen from the fruit, because once fallen, one must surely regain it in a mere moment. As the Sūtra (sūtra) says: "Bhikṣus (bhikṣu), you should know that if such a learned (bahu-śruta) noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka) loses right mindfulness (samyak smṛti), he is able to quickly return and cause that which arose from the fall to be exhausted, extinguished, and abandoned." If this were not so, the fruit of practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) would not be a secure place to be trusted. Furthermore, one who abides in the stage of the fruit does not perform actions (karman) that are contrary to that fruit; because their sense of shame has increased, they do not commit such acts even when temporarily fallen, just as a strong man, though he stumbles, does not fall. As stated above, there are those who, by refining their faculties, attain the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) or one in training (śaikṣa). When refining the faculties, how many paths of immediate result (ānantarya-mārga) and how many paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) are there for each? What is their nature (svabhāva) included in? What is their basis (āśraya)? The Verse says:

None who fall from the fruit will die before they have surely regained it;
They do not perform what is not done while abiding in the fruit,
For their shame has increased and thus they do not act so.
B: The Commentary says: There is no death in the interval of having fallen from the fruit (phala), because once fallen, one must surely regain it in a mere moment. As the Discourses (sūtra) say: "Bhikṣus, you should know that if such a learned noble disciple loses right mindfulness (smṛti), he is able to quickly return and cause that which arose from the fall to be exhausted, extinguished, and abandoned." If this were not so, the fruit of practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) would not be a secure place to be trusted. Furthermore, one who abides in the state of the fruit does not perform actions contrary to that fruit; because their shame (hrī) has increased, they do not commit such acts even when temporarily fallen, just as a strong man, though he stumbles, does not fall. As stated above, there are those who, by refining their faculties (indriya), attain the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) or one in training (śaikṣa). When they are in the process of refining their faculties, how many paths of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) and how many paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) are there for each? What nature (svabhāva) are they included in? What is their basis (āśraya)? The Verse says:

source: 「若於此五恐怖罪怨對休息、於三法決定離疑惑、於聖意如實知見，是聖弟子能自記說：『我地獄盡，畜生、餓鬼惡趣盡，得須陀洹，不墮惡趣法，決定正趣三菩提，七有天人往生，究竟苦邊。』」
A: “If one has ceased from these five terrifying sins and enmities, is firmly free from doubt regarding the three truths, and possesses knowledge and vision (jñāna-darśana) of the noble intent as it really is (yathābhūtam), that noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka) is able to declare of himself: ‘My hell is ended; the animal realm and the hungry ghost realm—the evil destinies (apāya)—are ended. I have attained the stream-enterer (srotaāpanna) state, I am not subject to the law of falling into evil destinies, I am firmly destined for full awakening (sambodhi), I will wander for at most seven existences among gods and humans (deva-manuṣya), and I will reach the complete ending (niṣṭhā) of suffering.’”
B: “If one has ceased from these five terrifying acts of enmity, is firmly free from doubt regarding the three teachings (tri-dharma), and truly sees and knows the noble intent (ārya-abhiprāya), this noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka) is able to declare of himself: ‘My hell is ended; the animal realm and the hungry ghost realm—the evil destinies (durgati)—are ended. I have attained the stream-enterer (srotāpanna), I am not subject to falling into an evil destiny, I am firmly destined for full awakening (sambodhi), and after at most seven existences of being reborn among gods and humans, I will reach the complete ending of suffering (duḥkha).’”

source: 論曰：若時菩薩於所緣境，無分別智都無所得，不取種種戲論相故，爾時乃名實住唯識真勝義性，即證真如智與真如平等平等，俱離能取、所取相故，能、所取相，俱是分別，有所得心，戲論現故。
A: The treatise says: When a Bodhisattva (bodhisattva), with regard to an object of cognition (ālambana), possesses non-discriminative wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) and attains absolutely nothing, because they do not grasp at the various signs of conceptual proliferation (prapañca), at that time it is called truly dwelling in the nature of the true ultimate reality (paramārtha-svabhāva) of Consciousness-Only (vijñapti-mātra). This is because the wisdom that realizes True Suchness (tathatā) and True Suchness itself are equal and identical, both being free from the characteristics of the grasper (grāhaka) and the grasped (grāhya). The characteristics of the grasper and the grasped are both conceptual constructions (vikalpa), because a mind that attains an object manifests as conceptual proliferation.
B: The treatise says: When a Bodhisattva (bodhisattva), with regard to an object of cognition (ālambana), possesses non-discriminative wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) and attains absolutely nothing (anupalambha), it is because they do not grasp at the various signs of conceptual proliferation (prapañca). At that time, it is called truly dwelling in the nature of the true ultimate reality (paramārtha) of Consciousness-Only; that is, the wisdom that realizes True Suchness (tathatā) and True Suchness itself are equal and identical, for both are free from the characteristics of the grasper (grāhaka) and the grasped (grāhya). The characteristics of both the grasper and the grasped are conceptual construction (vikalpa), because the mind that attains an object (upalambha) manifests as conceptual proliferation.

source: 論曰：前已廣說諸煩惱斷，由見諦道及修道故。道唯無漏亦有漏耶？見道應知唯是無漏，修道通二。所以者何？見道速能治三界故。頓斷九品見所斷故，非世間道有此堪能，故見位中道唯無漏。修道有異故通二種，如向所言由見諦故。此所見諦其相云何？頌曰：
A: The treatise says: It has already been extensively explained that the abandonment of all defilements (kleśa) occurs through the path of seeing the truths (darśana-mārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga). Are these paths only undefiled (anāsrava), or are they also defiled (sāsrava)? It should be known that the path of seeing is only undefiled, while the path of cultivation encompasses both. Why is this? Because the path of seeing is able to swiftly remedy the three realms (tridhātu) and abruptly abandon the nine grades of what is to be abandoned by seeing; worldly paths lack this capacity, and therefore, in the stage of seeing, the path is only undefiled. Because the path of cultivation is diverse, it encompasses both kinds, as previously stated regarding the seeing of the truths. What is the nature of these truths that are seen? The verse says:
B: The treatise says: It has already been extensively explained that the abandonment of all defilements (kleśa) comes about through the path of seeing the truths and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga). Are these paths only undefiled (anāsrava), or are they also defiled (āsrava)? It should be known that the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) is only undefiled, while the path of cultivation includes both. For what reason? Because the path of seeing is able to swiftly remedy the three realms (traidhātuka). Because it abruptly abandons the nine grades of what is to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-prahā), and the worldly path (laukika-mārga) does not possess this capability, therefore, in the stage of seeing, the path is only undefiled. Because the path of cultivation is different, it includes two kinds (dvividha), as was stated previously regarding the seeing of the truths. What is the nature of these truths that are seen? The verse says:

source: 云何漸次悟入唯識？謂諸菩薩於識相、性，資糧位中能深信解；在加行位能漸伏除所取、能取，引發真見；在通達位如實通達；修習位中如所見理，數數修習伏斷餘障；至究竟位出障圓明，能盡未來化有情類，復令悟入唯識相、性。
A: How does one gradually awaken to and enter Consciousness-Only (vijñapti-mātra)? It means that Bodhisattvas, during the stage of provisioning (sambhāra), are able to deeply believe in and understand the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and nature (svabhāva) of consciousness; during the stage of applied effort (prayoga), they are able to gradually subdue and eliminate the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka) to induce true vision (darśana); during the stage of realization (pratipatti), they realize these as they truly are (yathābhūtam); during the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā), they repeatedly practice in accordance with the principles they have perceived to subdue and sever the remaining hindrances; and upon arriving at the ultimate stage (niṣṭhā), they emerge from obstacles with perfect clarity, able to transform all classes of sentient beings (sattva-nikāya) until the end of time (anāgata), and cause them to awaken to and enter the characteristics and nature of Consciousness-Only.
B: How does one gradually awaken to and enter into Consciousness-Only (vijñaptimātra)? It is said that Bodhisattvas, while in the stage of provisioning (saṃbhāra-mārga), are able to deeply believe in and understand the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and nature (svabhāva) of consciousness. In the stage of applied effort (prayoga-mārga), they are able to gradually subdue and eliminate the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka), thereby inducing true vision. In the stage of realization (prativedha-mārga), they realize these as they truly are. In the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), they repeatedly practice in accordance with the principles they have perceived, in order to subdue and sever the remaining hindrances (āvaraṇa). Upon arriving at the ultimate stage (niṣṭhā-mārga), they emerge from all hindrances with perfect clarity, able to transform all classes of sentient beings until the end of time, and further cause them to awaken to and enter into the characteristics and nature of Consciousness-Only.

source: 論曰：經說通行總有四種：一苦遲通行、二苦速通行、三樂遲通行、四樂速通行。道依根本四靜慮生名樂通行，以攝受支止觀平等任運轉故。道依無色、未至、中間名苦通行，以不攝支止觀不等艱辛轉故。謂無色定觀減止增，未至、中間觀增止減。即此樂苦二通行中，鈍根名遲、利根名速。二行於境通達稽遲故名遲通，翻此名速。或遲鈍者所起通行名遲通行，速此相違。道亦名為菩提分法。此有幾種？名義云何？頌曰：
A: The treatise says: The scriptures state that there are four kinds of modes of progress (pratipad): first, the painful mode with slow realization; second, the painful mode with quick realization; third, the pleasant mode with slow realization; and fourth, the pleasant mode with quick realization. A path arising in reliance on the four fundamental meditative absorptions (catur-dhyāna) is called a "pleasant mode of progress," because it incorporates the factors of absorption and because tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) are balanced, allowing it to proceed effortlessly. A path relying on the formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti), the threshold state, or the intermediate state is called a "painful mode of progress," because it does not incorporate those factors, and because tranquility and insight are unequal, causing it to proceed with hardship. Specifically, in the formless absorptions, insight is diminished and tranquility is increased, whereas in the threshold and intermediate states, insight is increased and tranquility is diminished. Within these two modes of progress, the pleasant and the painful, those with dull faculties are termed "slow," while those with sharp faculties are termed "quick." Because these two modes of progress are slow in realizing their objects, they are called "slow progress," and the opposite of this is called "quick." Alternatively, the progress undertaken by one who is dull-witted is called "slow progress," and "quick" is the opposite of this. The path is also called the factors of awakening (bodhi-pakṣya). How many kinds of these are there, and what is the meaning of their names? The verse says:
B:
The treatise says: The sutras state that there are four kinds of routes (pratipad): first, the difficult route with slow realization (duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā); second, the difficult route with quick realization (duḥkhā pratipad kṣiprābhijñā); third, the easy route with slow realization (sukhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā); and fourth, the easy route with quick realization (sukhā pratipad kṣiprābhijñā).

A path arising in reliance on the four fundamental meditative absorptions (dhyāna) is called an "easy route," because it incorporates the factors of the absorption, and because tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) are balanced, allowing it to proceed effortlessly. A path relying on the formless attainments (ārūpya), the threshold state (anāgamya), or the intermediate absorption (dhyānāntara) is called a "difficult route," because it does not incorporate those factors, and because tranquility and insight are unequal, causing it to proceed with hardship. Specifically, in the formless attainments, insight is diminished and tranquility is increased, while in the threshold state and the intermediate absorption, insight is increased and tranquility is diminished.

Within these two modes of progress, the pleasant and the painful, those with dull faculties (mṛdvindriya) are termed "slow," while those with sharp faculties (tīkṣṇendriya) are termed "quick." Because the two modes of progress reach their object with delay, they are called "slow," and the opposite of this is called "quick." Alternatively, the progress undertaken by one who is dull-witted is called "slow progress," and "quick" is the opposite of this. The path is also called the factors of awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma). How many kinds are there? What are their names and meanings? The verse says:

source: 汝應諦聽：若唯一識，寧有十方凡聖、尊卑、因果等別？誰為誰說？何法何求？故「唯識」言有深意趣。「識」言總顯一切有情各有八識、六位心所，所變相、見、分位差別及彼空理所顯真如。識自相故，識相應故，二所變故，三分位故，四實性故，如是諸法皆不離識，總立識名。「唯」言，但遮愚夫所執定離諸識實有色等。
A: You should listen attentively: if there were only a single consciousness (vijñapti), how could there be distinctions such as the ten directions, the ordinary and the sacred, the venerable and the base, or cause and effect? Who would preach to whom? What dharma would be sought? Therefore, the term "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) has a profound intent. The word "consciousness" collectively reveals that all sentient beings each possess eight consciousnesses (vijñāna) and six categories of mental associates (caitta), the distinctions in the states of the "seen" (nimitta-bhāga) and "seeing" (darśana-bhāga) parts transformed from them, as well as the True Suchness (tathatā) revealed by the principle of emptiness (śūnyatā). Because of the self-nature of consciousness, because of the association of consciousness, because of the two transformations, because of the three states, and because of the four real natures, all such phenomena (dharma) are not separate from consciousness, and are thus collectively given the name "consciousness." The word "only" (mātra) simply excludes the real existence of form and other phenomena that the ignorant cling to as being definitely separate from the various consciousnesses.
B: You should listen well: if there were only a single consciousness, how could there be distinctions such as the ten directions (daśan-diś), the ordinary and the sacred, the venerable and the base, or cause and effect (hetu-phala)? Who would preach to whom? What dharma would be sought? Therefore, the term "consciousness-only" has a profound intent. The word "consciousness" (vijñāna) collectively reveals that all sentient beings (sarva-sattva) each possess eight consciousnesses and six categories of mental associates, the distinctions in the states (avasthā-bheda) of the transformed "seen" and "seeing" parts, as well as the True Suchness (tathatā) revealed by the principle of emptiness. Because of the self-nature (sva-lakṣaṇa) of consciousness, because of the association of consciousness (vijñāna-saṃprayuj), because of the two types of transformation, because of the three types of states, and because of the four types of ultimate reality, all such dharmas (sarva-dharma) are not separate from consciousness, and are thus collectively given the name "consciousness." The word "only" simply excludes the real existence of form (rūpa) and other phenomena that the ignorant (bāla) cling to as being definitely separate from the various consciousnesses.

source: 論曰：諸靜慮地所繫善法，由二緣捨：一由易地，謂從下地生上地時，或上地沒來生下地；二由得退，謂從已獲勝定功德還退失時。等言為顯捨眾同分亦捨少分殊勝善根，如色界中所有善法由易地退捨，無色界亦然，唯無律儀與色界異。無漏善法由三緣捨：一由得果，謂得果時捨前向道及果道故；二由練根，謂練根位由得利道捨鈍道故；三由退失，謂得退時退失果道勝果道故。如是已說捨諸律儀。不律儀云何捨？頌曰：
A:
The treatise says: Wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma) bound to the planes of meditative concentration (dhyāna-bhūmika) are abandoned for two reasons: first, by changing planes, which means when one is born from a lower plane into a higher plane, or when one dies in a higher plane and is reborn in a lower plane; second, by falling away, which means when one falls away from the merits (guṇa) of a superior concentration one has already attained. The word "etc." is used to indicate that one also abandons the shared group (nikāya-sabhāga) and abandons a small portion of superior wholesome roots (kuśala-mūla). Just as all wholesome dharmas in the form realm (rūpadhātu) are abandoned through changing planes or falling away, the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu) is the same, except that it lacks discipline (saṃvara), which differs from the form realm.

Wholesome dharmas that are undefiled (anāsrava) are abandoned for three reasons: first, by attaining a fruit, which means that at the time of attaining a fruit, one abandons the preceding path of the candidate and the path of the previous fruit; second, by refining the faculties, which means that at the stage of refining the faculties, one abandons the dull path by obtaining the sharp path; third, by falling away, which means that when one experiences a falling away, one loses the path of the fruit or the path of a superior fruit.

Thus, the abandonment of all discipline has been explained. How is non-discipline (asaṃvara) abandoned? The stanza says:
B:
The treatise says: The wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma) bound to the stages of meditative concentration (dhyāna-bhūmi) are abandoned for two reasons: first, by changing planes (bhūmi-saṃkrama), which means when one is born from a lower plane into a higher plane, or when one passes away from a higher plane and is reborn in a lower plane; second, by falling away (parihāṇi), which means when one falls away from the merits of a superior concentration (dhyāna-guṇa) that one has already attained. The word "etc." is used to indicate that one also abandons the shared characteristics (nikāya-sabhāga) and certain specific superior wholesome roots (kuśala-mūla). Just as all wholesome dharmas in the form realm (rūpa-dhātu) are abandoned through changing planes or falling away, the same is true for the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu), except that there is no discipline (saṃvara) there, which differs from the form realm.

Wholesome dharmas that are undefiled (anāsrava-dharma) are abandoned for three reasons: first, by attaining a fruit (phala-prāpti), meaning that when one attains a fruit, one abandons the preceding path of the candidate (pratipannaka-mārga) and the path of the previous fruit; second, by refining the faculties (indriya-saṃśodhana), meaning that at the stage of refining the faculties, one abandons the dull path (mṛdv-indriya-mārga) by obtaining the sharp path (tīkṣṇ-indriya-mārga); third, by falling away, meaning that when one experiences a falling away, one loses the path of the fruit or the path of a superior fruit.

Thus, the abandonment of the various disciplines has been explained. How is non-discipline (asaṃvara) abandoned? The stanza says:

source: 佛告婆羅門出家：「有三種婆羅門真實，我自覺悟成等正覺而復為人演說。汝婆羅門出家作如是說：『不害一切眾生，是婆羅門真諦，非為虛妄。』彼於彼言我勝、言相似、言我卑，若於彼真諦不繫著，於一切世間作慈心色像，是名第一婆羅門真諦，我自覺悟成等正覺，為人演說。
A: The Buddha said to the brahmin who had gone forth: “There are three kinds of brahmin truths that I have awakened to by myself, attained complete and perfect awakening (samyaksambodhi), and then explained to others. You, brahmin who have gone forth, speak thus: ‘Not harming any living being is the true reality (satya) of a brahmin, and it is not false.’ If one does not cling to that truth by saying ‘I am superior,’ ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’ in relation to others, but instead manifests a mind of loving-kindness (maitrī) toward the entire world, this is called the first brahmin truth, which I have awakened to by myself, attained complete and perfect awakening, and explained to others.”
B: The Buddha said to the brahmin (brāhmaṇa) who had gone forth (pravrajita): “There are three kinds of true brahmins, which I have realized for myself (pratyātma) and attained complete perfect awakening (abhisaṃbodhi), and which I now explain to others. You, brahmin who has gone forth, speak thus: ‘Not harming any living being (sarva-sattva) is the true reality of a brahmin, and it is not false.’ If one does not cling to that true reality—whether one says of others that ‘I am superior,’ ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’—and if one maintains a disposition of loving-kindness (maitra-citta) toward all the world (sarva-loka), this is called the first true reality of a brahmin, which I have realized for myself and attained complete perfect awakening, and which I explain to others.”

source: 如何道諦實能感苦？誰言實感？不爾，如何？無漏定、願，資有漏業，令所得果，相續長時，展轉增勝，假說名感。如是感時，由所知障為緣助力，非獨能感。然所知障，不障解脫，無能發業潤生用故。
A: How is it that the truth of the path (mārga-satya) can truly induce suffering? Who says it truly induces it? It is not so. How then? Untainted (anāsrava) meditative concentration and aspiration support tainted (āsrava) action (karma), causing the resulting fruit (phala) to continue (saṃtāna) for a long time (dīrgha-kāla), increasing and flourishing in succession (paramparā); it is metaphorically said to be "inducing." When it induces in this way, it is due to the cognitive obstacles (jñeyāvaraṇa) acting as a contributing condition (pratyaya); they cannot induce it alone. However, the cognitive obstacles do not obstruct liberation (vimokṣa), because they lack the function of initiating action and nourishing rebirth.
B: How does the path-truth (mārgasatya) truly induce suffering? Who says it truly induces it? It is not so. How then? The undefiled meditative absorption (anāsravasamādhi) and aspiration (praṇidhāna) support tainted karma (sāsravakarman), causing the resulting fruit to continue for a long time, extending and increasing in intensity; this is metaphorically called "inducing." When it induces in this way, it is due to the cognitive obstacles (jñeyāvaraṇa) acting as a contributing condition; they cannot induce it alone. However, the cognitive obstacles do not obstruct liberation, because they lack the function of initiating karma or nourishing rebirth.

source: 「聚落主！何等為三種卑下、田舍、常人凡夫樂受欲樂？有受欲者，非法濫取，不以安樂自供，不供養父母、給足兄弟、妻子、奴婢、眷屬、朋友、知識，亦不隨時供養沙門、婆羅門、仰求勝處安樂果報、未來生天，是名世間第一受欲。
A: "Village headman! What are the three kinds of base, rustic, and common worldly pleasures of sense-desire (kāma)? There is one who, while experiencing sense-desires, acquires them through unlawful means, does not provide for his own comfort, does not support his parents, provide for his brothers, wife, servants, dependents, friends, or acquaintances, and does not at the proper time make offerings to renunciants (śramaṇa) and brāhmaṇas (brāhmaṇa) while seeking the fruit of happiness in a superior realm or a future birth in heaven; this is called the first worldly pleasure of sense-desire."
B: "Village headman! What are the three kinds of base, rustic, and common worldling (pṛthagjana) enjoyments of sensual pleasure? There is one who enjoys sensual pleasure, who acquires it through unrighteousness (adharma), who does not provide for his own happiness, who does not make offerings (pūjā) to his parents, nor provide for his brothers, wife, children, servants, attendants, friends, or acquaintances, and who also does not at the proper time make offerings to renunciants (śramaṇa) or brāhmaṇas (brāhmaṇa), nor seek the fruit of happiness (phala-vipāka) in higher realms or future rebirth in heaven; this is called the first worldly (laukika-agra) enjoyment of sensual pleasure."

source: 須臾默然思惟已，語尊者那伽達多言：「青者謂戒也，白覆謂解脫也，一輻者身念也，轉者轉出也，車者止觀也，離結者有三種結，謂貪、恚、癡。彼阿羅漢諸漏已盡、已滅、已知、已斷根本，如截多羅樹頭更不復生，未來世滅不起法。
A: After remaining silent for a moment in contemplation, he said to the venerable (sthavira) Nāgadatta: "The blue refers to moral discipline (śīla), the white covering refers to liberation (vimokṣa), the single spoke refers to mindfulness of the body (kāya-smṛti), the turning refers to turning away, and the chariot refers to serenity and insight (śamatha-vipaśyanā). Being free from fetters (saṃyojana) refers to the three kinds of fetters, namely greed, hatred, and delusion. That worthy one (arhant) has exhausted all influxes (āsrava), they are extinguished, known, and their root is cut off, like cutting off the crown of a Palmyra tree so that it will not grow again, a phenomenon that is extinguished and does not arise in the future (anāgata-adhvan)."
B: After remaining silent for a moment in contemplation, he said to the Venerable Nāgadatta: "The blue refers to moral discipline (śīla), the white covering refers to liberation (vimukti), the single spoke refers to mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati), the turning refers to turning away, and the chariot refers to serenity and insight (śamathavipaśyanā). As for being free from fetters (saṃyojana), there are three kinds of fetters: greed (lobha), hatred (dveṣa), and delusion (moha). That arhat has exhausted all influxes (āsrava), they are extinguished, known, and their roots have been cut off, just like cutting off the crown of a Palmyra tree so that it will not grow again, a phenomenon that is extinguished and will not arise in the future."

source: 「聚落主！何等為三種卑下、田舍、常人凡夫樂受欲樂？有受欲者，非法濫取，不以安樂自供，不供養父母、給足兄弟、妻子、奴婢、眷屬、朋友、知識，亦不隨時供養沙門、婆羅門、仰求勝處安樂果報、未來生天，是名世間第一受欲。
A: "Village headman! What are the three kinds of base, rustic, and common worldly pleasures of sense-desire (kāma)? There is one who, while experiencing sense-desires, acquires them through unlawful means, does not provide for his own comfort, does not support his parents, provide for his brothers, wife, servants, dependents, friends, or acquaintances, and does not at the proper time make offerings to renunciants (śramaṇa) and brāhmaṇas (brāhmaṇa) while seeking the fruit of happiness in a superior realm or a future birth in heaven; this is called the first worldly pleasure of sense-desire."
B: "Village headman! What are the seven kinds of base, rustic, and common worldly pleasures of sense-desire (kāma)? There is one who, while experiencing sense-desires, acquires them through unlawful means, does not provide for his own comfort, does not support his parents, provide for his brothers, wife, servants, dependents, friends, or acquaintances, and does not at the proper time make offerings to renunciants (śramaṇa) and brāhmaṇas (brāhmaṇa) while seeking the fruit of happiness in a superior realm or a future birth in heaven; this is called the first worldly pleasure of sense-desire."
